title: When Satisfaction and Clinical Outcome Disagree: Understanding Discordance Between Patient Experience and Psychiatric Treatment Response—A Narrative Review
content: Patient satisfaction and patient-reported experience are widely used as indicators of the quality of mental health care and, implicitly, as proxies for treatment benefit, whereas clinical outcome is usually judged from clinician-rated symptom scales. This narrative review examines whether, and why, these two assessments diverge in psychiatric treatment. It clarifies the constructs of satisfaction, experience and outcome; examines measurement- and rater-level sources of apparent disagreement; synthesises studies that directly compare patient- and clinician-derived assessments; and proposes an explanatory framework. Associations between satisfaction and clinician-rated outcome are consistently positive but small: in one acute-care study, experience of care accounted for less than 7% of the variance in symptom change, and patient–clinician agreement about the same care episode was low. Patients and clinicians judge improvement from different frames of reference, while ceiling effects, social desirability and fixed thresholds for meaningful change further distort comparison. Seven mechanisms sustain divergence: expectancy, therapeutic alliance, insight, subjective tolerability, decisional involvement, perceived coercion and the conceptual gap between symptom remission and personal recovery; each shapes satisfaction largely independently of symptom change. Satisfaction and clinical outcome are therefore related but non-interchangeable constructs. Services should measure both, adjust satisfaction scores for patient characteristics, and treat discordance as clinically informative rather than as error. Shared decision-making, honest expectation management, reduction of perceived coercion and recovery-oriented care are the most plausible routes to aligning patient experience with clinical outcome.
